title: Many Japanese Workers Consider Quitting Their Jobs
paragraphs: In the past, many Japanese workers stayed with one company for their whole career. But today, a lot of workers in Japan are thinking about leaving their jobs, and their reasons are changing.

According to a survey by the recruitment company Randstad, the top reason Japanese workers leave their jobs is now to improve their work-life balance. The survey was carried out in January 2026 and included 4,464 people aged 18 to 65. About 33% of people said they left a job to get a better work-life balance, while 31% said it was because their pay was too low. This is the first time work-life balance has been the number one reason. Pay had been the top reason for the previous three years.

Many other workers are also unhappy but are staying in their jobs. A survey by Mynavi, a job information company, found that 46.7% of regular employees in Japan are "quiet quitting." This means they only do the minimum amount of work required and do not try to do more.

Some workers who want to quit find it hard to tell their boss. In Japan, quitting a job can be very uncomfortable, especially when bosses try to stop workers from leaving. Because of this, some people pay special companies called "resignation agencies" to quit for them. According to Mynavi, nearly one in five people in their 20s who quit their jobs last year used a service like this.

Together, these surveys suggest that many Japanese workers now care more about their private lives and their well-being than about pay alone. For companies that want to keep their workers, offering a better balance between work and life may be just as important as offering a higher salary.
